White, churchgoers say, stands for gratitude and renewal. Those not in church count down in pubs, hotels and clubs with music and food, or stay quietly at home with family, sending good wishes.

For Accra the night is the finale of “Detty December”: from mid-December the capital lives on concerts and parties, and since the 2019 “Year of Return” the diaspora flies in for the holidays. Accra’s Anglican Cathedral of the Most Holy Trinity welcomed 2026 with an all-night service, its congregation dressed in white.

traditions.title: Church until dawn
traditions.text: On 31 December churches fill up in the evening: hymns, testimonies and prayers go on past midnight into the first hours of the new year.

traditions.title: Dressed in white
traditions.text: Many wear white to the night service, as a sign of gratitude for the year behind, of renewal and of good intentions for the one ahead.

traditions.title: Countdown to music
traditions.text: Those not in church meet midnight in pubs, hotels and clubs with music; in the pubs of Tema, near Accra, drinks come with kebabs and grilled guinea fowl.

meta.title: New Year in Ghana: Accra | Time2Fest
meta.description: Ghana meets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: watch night services in white, hymns until dawn, countdowns in Accra’s clubs and the grand finale of Detty December.

GL.text:
Midnight comes twice here: at 21:00 local time the New Year reaches Denmark, so it can be greeted once, and then again at midnight, this time Greenland's own. The holiday falls in the polar night, when the day is a few hours of twilight, snow is a certainty and a red-orange Christmas star still glows in almost every window. The stars come down only on 6 January, the same day the mitaartut make their rounds: silent masked visitors who are treated to cakes and sweets.

Nuuk meets midnight at 02:00 UTC. The last rockets are bought right before the evening, no party goes without funny hats, and at midnight the sky over the town turns thick with firework smoke. People shake hands and wish each other 'Ukiortaami pilluaritsi!', 'Be happy at the New Year!'.

traditions.title: Two New Years in one evening
traditions.text: At 21:00 local time it is midnight in Denmark, so the New Year is greeted twice: the second time at midnight, Greenland time.

traditions.title: Rockets in the polar night
traditions.text: At midnight rockets and firework batteries go up over Nuuk, while people shake hands and wish each other a happy New Year.

traditions.title: Masked mitaartut
traditions.text: Around 6 January silent masked visitors knock on doors, make their hosts laugh without a word and are rewarded with cakes and sweets.

meta.title: New Year in Greenland: Nuuk | Time2Fest
meta.description: Nuuk greets 2027 at 02:00 UTC: Greenland celebrates twice, at 21:00 with Denmark and again at midnight, with rockets in the polar night and handshakes.

BF.text:
"Bonne année!" — at midnight people hug and say it both in church and at a maquis table. About two thirds of Burkina Faso is Muslim and over a quarter Christian, so many see in the year at a night service and only then join friends; 1 January is a day off for everyone. In recent years the most common New Year's wish has been for peace.

Ouagadougou glows with garlands for the occasion, and people walk the streets in their best clothes. The maquis — open-air grill cafés with music — bring in extra chairs and waiters, and the dancing goes on until 2 a.m. and later. At work the holiday stretches through January: teams gather for the "présentation de vœux", the New Year greetings — once with food and drink, now often more modestly.

traditions.title: The night service
traditions.text: Believers meet midnight in church: prayer and singing, and as soon as the clock shows 00:00, hugs and "Bonne année!". After the service some still go out dancing.

traditions.title: A night at the maquis
traditions.text: The maquis, open-air grill cafés with music, are packed on New Year's Eve: people dance there at midnight, and the busiest stay open until 2 a.m.

traditions.title: January greetings
traditions.text: Throughout January, workplaces hold a "présentation de vœux": colleagues wish each other a happy new year and talk about plans, sometimes over food and drink.

meta.title: New Year in Burkina Faso: Ouagadougou | Time2Fest
meta.description: Burkina Faso meets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: Ouagadougou greets midnight with "Bonne année!" in church, dances in the maquis until 2 a.m. and glows with garlands.

GW.text:
The year turns here at 00:00 UTC, the same moment as on the prime meridian: Guinea-Bissau keeps Greenwich time all year round. It is one of the most religiously diverse countries in the world, with about half the people Muslim and most of the rest Catholic or followers of traditional beliefs, so the winter holidays are shared. 1 January is a public holiday: families and communities sit down to a shared meal of rice with peanut caldo de mancarra or palm-oil sigá, with palm wine on the table.

In Bissau the end-of-year season starts with Christmas: Catholics go to midnight mass, salt cod is cooked on charcoal stoves right in the street, and food is shared with neighbours and friends; even Muslims join in. The city's big street carnival comes in February.

traditions.title: Midnight on Greenwich time
traditions.text: Guinea-Bissau never changes its clocks, so the new year arrives here at 00:00 UTC, together with the prime meridian.

traditions.title: A shared table on 1 January
traditions.text: The first day of the year is a holiday: families and communities gather for a shared meal of rice with sauces and stews, washed down with palm wine.

traditions.title: Caldo de mancarra at home
traditions.text: Simmer a peanut sauce with chicken and serve it with rice: that is caldo de mancarra, a traditional dish of Guinea-Bissau.

meta.title: New Year in Guinea-Bissau: Bissau | Time2Fest
meta.description: Guinea-Bissau greets 2027 at 00:00 UTC, in step with Greenwich: a shared table on 1 January, caldo de mancarra and palm wine, and midnight mass in Bissau.

IS.text:
In Iceland, New Year rockets are bought from rescuers: from 28 December to 6 January fireworks are sold by ICE-SAR search-and-rescue teams, and the money pays for their training, equipment and vehicles. The evening starts around the family dinner table; at about half past eight bonfires known as brennur blaze up in neighbourhoods, and at half past ten most of the country laughs at «Áramótaskaupið», a satirical review of the year that has aired on New Year's Eve since the 1940s. Old belief says the elves move house tonight, so candles are left out to light their way.

Reykjavík meets midnight at 00:00 UTC with no single official show: rockets go up from every garden and street, and many people climb the hill to Hallgrímskirkja, where the sky around the spire flashes almost without a break.

traditions.title: Rockets from the rescuers
traditions.text: Fireworks are bought from ICE-SAR teams, so the money goes to rescue missions. At midnight families launch them straight from gardens and streets.

traditions.title: Brennur bonfires
traditions.text: Between 20:30 and 21:00 neighbours gather at bonfires in their districts, with songs and short speeches. If the wind tops 10 m/s, the fires are postponed.

traditions.title: A laugh at the year
traditions.text: Before midnight the country laughs at «Áramótaskaupið», a satire of the year’s events. Put a candle on the windowsill: folk belief says it guides the elves as they move house.

meta.title: New Year in Iceland: Reykjavík | Time2Fest
meta.description: Iceland greets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: rockets sold by rescue teams light up Reykjavík, brennur bonfires blaze in every district and fireworks ring Hallgrímskirkja.

GG.text:
In Guernsey the old year used to be buried at the stroke of midnight. Boys wrapped a log in black cloth, called it le vieux bout de l’an, “the old end of the year”, and carried it through the streets by the light of hollowed-out turnip lanterns like a funeral procession, before burying it on the beach or burning it on a bonfire. Children, meanwhile, went from door to door for a New Year gift called the oguinane, singing “Open your purse, then shut it again!” The word is often compared with the Scottish Hogmanay.

Today December on the island belongs to the sea. Until 31 December people dip into twelve festive bays to raise money for a hospice, on Christmas morning swimmers plunge into the La Vallette sea pools in St Peter Port, and on Boxing Day thousands of islanders wade together into the cold water of Cobo Bay.

traditions.title: Burying the old year
traditions.text: At midnight boys once carried a log wrapped in black, “the old end of the year”, through the streets by turnip lantern, then buried it on the beach or burned it.

traditions.title: The oguinane gift
traditions.text: Children went from door to door singing for a New Year present, the oguinane, a word often compared with the Scottish Hogmanay.

traditions.title: Winter sea dips
traditions.text: Until 31 December islanders dip into twelve festive bays for a hospice, and on Boxing Day thousands wade together into the sea at Cobo Bay.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Guernsey: St Peter Port | Time2Fest
meta.description: Guernsey greets 2027 at local midnight (00:00 UTC): the old torchlit burial of the year, the children's oguinane gift and December dips in a cold sea.

GM.text:
A paper boat glowing from within sails down the street to drums and songs: this is the fanal, and it is how The Gambia sees the year out. Almost all Gambians are Muslim, yet the season from Christmas to New Year belongs to everyone: Kankurang and Zimba masquerades, stilt walkers and “hunting” groups fill the streets, and many hotels set off fireworks on New Year’s Eve. Fanals, frames of bamboo and paper lit from inside, are carried until 1 or 2 January; New Year’s Day itself is a public holiday.

The capital gathers it all into the week-long Banjul Cultural Festival. Its 2025 programme had wrestlers competing on the beach on 31 December and fireworks at Arch 22 at midnight, and on 1 January more than fifty hunting societies with their masquerades paraded until dawn. An estimated 50,000 people came.

traditions.title: Fanal, the lantern boat
traditions.text: From mid-December to 1 or 2 January men carry a big paper boat lit from inside through the streets, while women lead the songs to the drums.

traditions.title: Masquerades until dawn
traditions.text: During the holiday week Kankurang, Zimba “lions” and stilt walkers roam the streets, and on 1 January hunting societies with masquerades dance in Banjul from morning until dawn.

traditions.title: Wrestling and fireworks
traditions.text: On the afternoon of 31 December wrestlers compete on Banjul Beach, and at midnight fireworks light up the sky above Arch 22 and many hotels along the coast.

meta.title: New Year in The Gambia: Banjul | Time2Fest
meta.description: The Gambia enters 2027 at 00:00 UTC: glowing paper fanal boats, Kankurang masquerades in the streets, beach wrestling and fireworks at Banjul’s Arch 22.

LR.text:
More than eight in ten Liberians are Christians, so the last evening of the year here belongs to Watch Night, the night vigil. Churches across the country fill up from the evening: a choir, drums and piano, a sermon and prayers of thanks for the year gone by. Seconds before twelve the pastor leads the countdown himself, and the moment midnight comes, quiet prayer bursts into dancing right between the rows. The first of January is a public holiday.

Monrovia sees the year in more loudly. On the night into 2015, when the Ebola curfew was lifted for a single night, music boomed from beer parlours, clubs and storefront churches all along Tubman Boulevard, car horns honked and people danced in the streets. On the morning of 1 January many head to the ocean beach, where roast chicken and smoked fish are sold at the gate.

traditions.title: The pastor’s countdown
traditions.text: At the Watch Night vigil the pastor counts down the last seconds before twelve, and with the first minute of the year the whole church starts dancing.

traditions.title: Music from every doorway
traditions.text: After midnight the beer parlours and clubs along Monrovia’s Tubman Boulevard play loud, cars honk and some people dance right in the street.

traditions.title: New Year’s Day by the sea
traditions.text: 1 January is a day off, and Monrovians relax by the ocean, sitting under thatch umbrellas with roast chicken and smoked fish.

meta.title: New Year in Liberia: Monrovia | Time2Fest
meta.description: Liberia greets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: Watch Night vigils with the pastor’s countdown, music along Monrovia’s Tubman Boulevard and the ocean beach on 1 January.

MA.text:
A log cake: few Moroccan families see out the old year without one. On the morning of 31 December people hurry to the pastry shops before the best ones sell out, and in the evening they gather round it at home. Some book a table at a restaurant, while squares and boulevards fill with families and groups of young people. New Year’s Day is a holiday. Two weeks later, on 14 January, comes Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year, a public holiday too since 2023. The table holds seven-vegetable dishes or tagoula, a porridge of barley or corn grits with honey and argan oil, with a date stone hidden inside for luck.

Casablanca, along with Marrakech and Fez, is one of the cities people travel to for New Year’s, with traditional music and dancing. Along the Atlantic runs the Ain Diab corniche, lined with hotels, restaurants and nightclubs.

traditions.title: A log cake by morning
traditions.text: Families hurry out for a log cake first thing in the morning, before it sells out, and gather round it at home in the evening.

traditions.title: Music and dancing in Casablanca
traditions.text: In Casablanca, Marrakech and Fez the night brings traditional music and dancing; on the Ain Diab corniche the restaurants and clubs stay lit.

traditions.title: Tagoula for Yennayer
traditions.text: On 14 January, the Amazigh New Year, families cook tagoula from barley or corn grits with honey; a date stone hidden inside brings luck.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Morocco: Casablanca | Time2Fest
meta.description: Morocco greets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: a morning dash for the log cake on 31 December, music and dancing in Casablanca, then Yennayer and tagoula on 14 January.

ML.text:
Chicken is the dish of the year's end: before 31 December Mali's markets fill with poultry, even if prices bite every year. Over 96% of Malians are Muslim, so 1 January is above all a public holiday, while Christian communities meet midnight at masses and prayer vigils. Firecrackers and fireworks are banned nationwide every December, so at midnight what matters is hugs and good wishes.

Bamako celebrates in its "grin", the circle of friends who meet right on the street. Young people pool money for a shared table and head to clubs, hotels or rented flats, and the countdown ends in hugs. Others stay home: on 31 December 2024 residents queued at banks to buy chickens, gifts for the children and a good dinner. Older people remember open-air dances to battery radios.

traditions.title: Chicken for the feast
traditions.text: Before 31 December the markets fill with poultry: chicken is Mali's year-end dish. Families buy it for the dinner even when prices bite.

traditions.title: Countdown with the grin
traditions.text: Young people meet midnight with their circle of friends: they pool money for a shared table, go to clubs or rented flats, and the last seconds end in hugs and wishes.

traditions.title: Mass and night vigil
traditions.text: Mali's Christian communities hold New Year masses and prayer vigils, giving thanks for the year that is ending and entrusting their hopes for the new one to God.

meta.title: New Year in Mali: Bamako | Time2Fest
meta.description: Mali greets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: Bamako enjoys a chicken feast, counts down with the grin, its circle of friends, and hugs at midnight; churches hold vigils.

GN.text:
Christmas and New Year’s Eve merge here into a single season, the ‘year-end festivities’: families get together, and 25 December and 1 January are public holidays. Most Guineans are Muslim (84% by a 2023 estimate, with 11% Christians), yet everyone sees in the New Year. Fireworks are off limits: for the 2025/26 holidays their sale and use were banned nationwide from 24 December to 5 January.

Conakry’s loudest night is the ‘Bal des Grands’: on 31 December 2025 the legendary Bembeya Jazz National, Mali’s Sidiki Diabaté and singer Djelykaba Bintou played, and it sold out for the fourth year in a row. On 1 January the city sails to the Îles de Los, two kilometres offshore, for beaches and forest; since 2024 the state has organised the crossings from the Sandervalia maritime station.

traditions.title: By boat to the Îles de Los
traditions.text: On 1 January many Conakry residents cross from the Kaloum ports to the Îles de Los to swim and walk in the forest; life jackets are handed out for the crossing.

traditions.title: Bal des Grands from 8 pm
traditions.text: Doors of the ball in Camayenne open at 8 pm, and all evening stars of African music play — from the veterans of Bembeya Jazz to young singers.

traditions.title: A family night, no firecrackers
traditions.text: From Christmas to New Year families gather, while the authorities ban firecrackers and beach concerts in Conakry for the holidays.

meta.title: New Year in Guinea: Conakry | Time2Fest
meta.description: Guinea greets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: Conakry’s Bal des Grands with Bembeya Jazz, family year-end festivities and boats to the Îles de Los on 1 January.

JE.text:
“Ma hodgîngnole!” Jersey people once cried this when asking for a New Year gift. The custom has long gone, but the word is compared with Norman hoguinané and Scottish Hogmanay. The season runs on until Twelfth Night, when islanders sing and drink to the health of the apple trees so they bear fruit. Before the 20th century cider was the backbone of the island’s economy, so the songs are often in Jèrriais, Jersey’s own Norman language.

There is no big public fireworks display at midnight: in 2026 islanders even signed a petition for New Year’s Eve fireworks at Elizabeth Castle. Instead, the night is lit by neighbours’ fireworks. And on 1 January long-distance swimmers walk into the winter sea at St Catherine’s slipway on the island’s east coast.

traditions.title: Songs for the apple trees
traditions.text: On Twelfth Night islanders sing in the orchards and drink to the apple trees’ health so they bear fruit, often with songs in Jèrriais.

traditions.title: The first swim of the year
traditions.text: On 1 January long-distance swimmers take to the sea at St Catherine’s slipway, and on Christmas Day hundreds of islanders swim in several bays for the hospice.

traditions.title: Neighbours’ fireworks
traditions.text: With no official display at midnight, private fireworks light the sky; after a popular show in St Aubin’s Bay, islanders are asking for New Year fireworks at Elizabeth Castle.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Jersey: St Helier | Time2Fest
meta.description: Jersey greets 2027 at local midnight (00:00 UTC): neighbours’ fireworks, wassail songs for the apple trees on Twelfth Night and a first swim in the winter sea.

IE.text:
In Irish, the last evening of the year is Oíche na Coda Móire, “the night of the big portion”: the family sits down to a generous dinner so that the new year will be well fed too. On that day nothing left the house — no food, no goods — and no water was drawn from the well after sunset. In some places a large barmbrack, a raisin bread, was baked: the man of the house took three bites and threw it against the inside of the front door to drive hunger away for the whole year, and the family gathered the pieces and ate them. Towards midnight bells rang, bonfires burned and people sang. Today the night is mostly spent at home, at small parties with family and friends.

For three days, from 30 December to 1 January, Dublin hands its streets to the NYF Dublin festival. The main stage is Dublin Castle: the evening Countdown Concert ends with the “Midnight Moment”, children get an afternoon concert, and on 1 January the castle hosts free concerts.

traditions.title: Night of the big portion
traditions.text: Families end the year with a generous dinner — a full table was meant to bring a full year, and nothing was carried out of the house that day.

traditions.title: Barmbrack at the door
traditions.text: The man of the house once took three bites of the New Year raisin bread and threw it at the front door to drive hunger away; the family ate the pieces.

traditions.title: Countdown at Dublin Castle
traditions.text: Dubliners meet midnight at the Countdown Concert in Dublin Castle, and on 1 January they come back for free afternoon concerts.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Ireland: Dublin | Time2Fest
meta.description: Ireland greets 2027 at local midnight (00:00 UTC): the night of the big portion, a barmbrack thrown at the door and the Countdown Concert at Dublin Castle.

MR.text:
Nouakchott's loudest fireworks of the year come not on 31 December but on the night of 28 November, when the army fires them from Liberty Square for Independence Day. In the Islamic Republic of Mauritania New Year is a secular holiday: 1 January is a day off, many people see in midnight, and some religious currents warn against the parties as a foreign custom. So the celebration mostly happens behind closed doors: the authorities license parties, and before 2020 began the Interior Ministry stepped up patrols and guarded hotels, restaurants and party halls.

Nouakchott gets ready at the markets. Back in 2012 Cridem described how, a week before 31 December, young people from every district crowded the Sebkha market looking for new outfits brought in from Senegal. Nightclubs were closed then, so groups of friends rented flats, and none were left free. Others see in midnight at home with family.

traditions.title: A night at a hotel or hall
traditions.text: New Year parties in Nouakchott take place in hotels, restaurants and party halls under official licences, while the police step up patrols for the night.

traditions.title: A new outfit from the market
traditions.text: A week before the holiday young people head to the Sebkha market for a new outfit for 31 December, often brought in from Senegal.

traditions.title: A flat for the whole night
traditions.text: Groups of friends rent flats for New Year's Eve, so hardly any are free by the day before. Others see in midnight at home with family.

meta.title: New Year in Mauritania: Nouakchott | Time2Fest
meta.description: Mauritania greets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: Nouakchott shops for new outfits at the Sebkha market, parties in hotels and halls and saves big fireworks for 28 November.

FK.text:
Midnight on 31 December in the Falkland Islands falls in the height of the southern summer: the sun sets after nine in the evening, and the sky never turns fully black before dawn. The islands are a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina. Fewer than four thousand people live here, so the holidays feel homely. The end of December is almost one long break: 25–27 December are public holidays, government offices close on 30 and 31 December, and 1 January is a day off again.

Stanley, home to most islanders, spends the festive week outdoors. On Christmas Eve carols are sung under the whalebone arch by Christ Church Cathedral, on 26–27 December the racecourse on the west side of town hosts horse races that have run for more than a century, and at New Year those who have built a raft of their own compete in a home-made raft race.

traditions.title: Races between the holidays
traditions.text: On 26 and 27 December Stanley gathers at the racecourse: the Christmas races have run for over a century, with gymkhanas between the heats.

traditions.title: Home-made raft race
traditions.text: The New Year raft race brings out everyone who has built a raft of their own: registration and inspection in the morning, the start at noon.

traditions.title: A bright New Year's night
traditions.text: On 31 December the sun sets around 9:10pm and rises before 4:40am, so the night is short: even at midnight the sky never turns fully black.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in the Falkland Islands: Stanley | Time2Fest
meta.description: The Falkland Islands greet 2027 at local midnight (03:00 UTC): a bright midsummer night, Christmas horse races in Stanley and a race of home-made rafts.

SH.text:
Midnight on St Helena was once marked by the ringing of handbells. Until 1941 the island kept solar time, so the New Year arrived here about 23 minutes later than in Britain. The holidays fall in the southern summer: between Christmas and New Year most offices close, and islanders visit family and friends, including Saints who have come home from overseas. Most Christmas decorations come down by 1 January.

The night is louder now. In Jamestown people dance on The Bridge by the seafront from the evening of 31 December until 2am and later, mostly to recorded music; some years local bands play and fireworks go up at midnight. 1 January is a public holiday, and sometimes that very day the yachts of the Governor's Cup race arrive at the island.

traditions.title: Dancing on The Bridge
traditions.text: Jamestown gathers by the seafront on the evening of 31 December and dances until 2am; some years local bands play and fireworks go up at midnight.

traditions.title: Ring a bell at midnight
traditions.text: Islanders once rang in the New Year with handbells. Find a little bell at home and ring it the moment midnight comes.

traditions.title: Yachts on New Year's Day
traditions.text: The Governor's Cup yacht race runs from late December into early January, so sailing yachts sometimes reach the island on 1 January itself.

meta.title: New Year 2027 on Saint Helena: Jamestown | Time2Fest
meta.description: Saint Helena greets 2027 at local midnight (00:00 UTC): dancing on The Bridge in Jamestown, a southern-summer night and the old custom of ringing handbells.

SN.text:
For most Senegalese, 31 December is not a religious holiday: about 95% of the population is Muslim, and in the Islamic calendar it is an ordinary day. Yet New Year’s Eve grows more popular every year. In December tailors work flat out as young people order evening dresses, suits and jackets for the 31st — “Tabaski and Korité are faith, the 31st is just the trend,” laughs one client. Markets sell out of chickens for the festive table, Catholic parishes gather for night prayer, and 1 January is a public holiday.

Dakar sees in midnight without a city fireworks show — there hasn’t been one for years — but firecrackers crackle through the neighbourhoods: family stalls sell “fire balls”, and children set them off with their parents until two or three in the morning. Many families welcomed 2024 on the decorated Place de l’Indépendance.

traditions.title: Chicken for the feast
traditions.text: Before Christmas and New Year, Dakar’s markets can hardly keep up with the demand for chickens: families snap them up for the festive table, just as they do before Korité.

traditions.title: Firecrackers until 3 a.m.
traditions.text: With no city fireworks, neighbourhoods greet midnight with firecrackers and small fireworks from family stalls, which children light together with their parents.

traditions.title: Night prayer in parishes
traditions.text: Catholics see in the year at their parishes with New Year’s Eve vigils of prayer and talks about peace, and on 1 January the whole country has a day off.

meta.title: New Year in Senegal: Dakar | Time2Fest
meta.description: Senegal welcomes 2027 at 00:00 UTC: new outfits from Dakar’s tailors, chicken on the festive table, firecrackers in the streets and night prayer in parishes.

ST.text:
In São Tomé and Príncipe the old year is washed away in the sea. On the morning of 1 January people from all over the country head to the beaches for the traditional "washing of the year" (lavagem do ano), to step into the new one renewed. The night before is loud: every year the police note plenty of firecrackers and fireworks nationwide. The new day brings the President's New Year address and news of the "baby of the year": in 2023 a boy was born at 00:05.

The capital welcomed 2026 with a festival right on the beach facing the National Radio, drawing people in from the outskirts too. In the morning the party moves to Praia da Ilha by the National Museum, where stalls sell fruit, snacks and island dishes between swims, music plays and coast guard lifeguards keep watch from the water.

traditions.title: Wash the old year away
traditions.text: From the first hours of 1 January the beaches fill up: people from all over the country wade into the sea to "wash" the old year away and start the new one renewed.

traditions.title: Firecrackers at midnight
traditions.text: The night of 1 January is loud: people set off firecrackers and fireworks all over the country, and the police mention it every year in their holiday-night reports.

traditions.title: A beach party in the capital
traditions.text: São Tomé met 2026 with a festival on the beach facing the National Radio, and in the morning Praia da Ilha has stalls of fruit, snacks and island dishes to music.

meta.title: New Year in São Tomé and Príncipe: São Tomé | Time2Fest
meta.description: São Tomé and Príncipe greets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: firecrackers at midnight, a beach festival in the capital and a sea swim on 1 January to wash the old year away.

CV.text:
As soon as night falls on 31 December, people in Mindelo on São Vicente pick up the racordai — a wooden shaker studded with flattened bottle caps — to sing New Year greetings, then dance until dawn. Emigrants from Europe and the USA fly home to Cape Verde for the holidays: Boston–Praia flights can be sold out by early December. Towns on Santiago island put on free concerts with fireworks, and in São Filipe on Fogo island the year is even welcomed on a beach of black volcanic sand.

The capital’s big open-air party is the “Virada de Ano” at Quebra Canela: artists perform from 10 pm until 4 am, and fireworks light up the sky over the beach. For something cosier there are bars and restaurants — at the end of 2025 Praia’s hotels were 80–90 % full.

traditions.title: Racordai and greetings
traditions.text: On the evening of 31 December Mindelo shakes the racordai, a wooden rattle with bottle caps, and sings “boas festas”, the season’s greetings.

traditions.title: Concert and fireworks
traditions.text: Towns hold free open-air concerts — in Praia, Assomada, Santa Cruz and São Filipe — and at midnight fireworks rise over the squares.

traditions.title: Home for the holidays
traditions.text: For Christmas and New Year emigrants return from Europe and the USA to celebrate with family, so flights and hotels fill up.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Cape Verde: Praia | Time2Fest
meta.description: Cape Verde welcomes 2027 at local midnight (01:00 UTC): racordai rattles and songs in Mindelo, an open-air concert with fireworks in Praia, emigrants home.

GS.text:
South Georgia has no permanent residents, so the New Year is seen in by whoever is working on the island that summer: government officers and their families, British Antarctic Survey scientists at two stations and museum staff who come for the season. Midnight falls at 02:00 UTC, and it never gets truly dark: at the end of December the sun sets around half past eight in the evening and the sky stays in twilight until morning. The big polar holiday is Midwinter in June, while 1 January falls in the busiest season, when expedition ships call. The islands are a British Overseas Territory that Argentina also claims.

About twenty people live at King Edward Point. Nearby in Grytviken, the white wooden whalers' church, consecrated on Christmas Day 1913, still holds an occasional service, and visitors from the ships walk up to Ernest Shackleton's grave.

traditions.title: Midnight without darkness
traditions.text: At the end of December the sun drops behind the mountains around 20:37 and is up again at 03:53, so the New Year arrives under a twilight sky.

traditions.title: The whalers' church
traditions.text: Consecrated on Christmas Day 1913, it is the only building of the whaling station still used as intended: services are held now and then, and couples have even married here.

traditions.title: Summer ship season
traditions.text: There is no airport, so guests arrive on expedition ships, about 80 visits a year, mostly in summer, and in Grytviken they walk to Shackleton's grave.

meta.title: New Year on South Georgia: Grytviken | Time2Fest
meta.description: South Georgia meets 2027 at 02:00 UTC with no permanent residents: scientists and officials near Grytviken, a twilight sky instead of night, a whalers' church.

PT.text:
At midnight Portugal counts more than the clock's strokes: it counts raisins too. There are twelve, one for each month of the year, each with a wish, followed by a glass of champagne. On the table these days sits bolo-rei, the 'king cake', a crown-shaped ring topped with candied fruit and nuts. A fava bean is hidden in the dough, and whoever finds it buys the cake next year.

Lisbon gathers by the Tagus on Praça do Comércio: concerts start at 21:30, and midnight is counted down on the clock of the Rua Augusta arch. At midnight fireworks blaze over the river for ten minutes, in 2025 together with 250 drones. And on the evening of 1 January the Lisbon Metropolitan Orchestra plays its New Year's concert in Belém.

traditions.title: Twelve raisins
traditions.text: At midnight, eat twelve raisins and make a wish on each, one for every month, then raise a glass of champagne.

traditions.title: Bolo-rei and the fava
traditions.text: Families cut the bolo-rei, a crown-shaped cake with candied fruit and nuts. Whoever finds the fava bean in their slice buys next year’s cake.

traditions.title: Fireworks over the Tagus
traditions.text: Lisboners gather on Praça do Comércio and the Cais do Sodré and Ribeira das Naus waterfronts, and at midnight fireworks blaze over the river for ten minutes.

meta.title: New Year in Portugal: Lisbon | Time2Fest
meta.description: Portugal greets 2027 at midnight, 00:00 UTC: in Lisbon it means twelve raisins with wishes, bolo-rei and ten minutes of fireworks over the Tagus.

SL.text:
Many people in Sierra Leone spend the first hours of the year in church or another place of worship, while others choose beach bars, cafés and nightclubs. Nearly eight in ten people here are Muslim and about a fifth are Christian, and the holidays of both faiths are national ones, so on 1 January the whole country has the day off. Don’t expect a midnight barrage: for the festive season police ban fireworks nationwide, and loud music in neighbourhoods after ten at night.

In these days Freetown is drawn to the ocean. Thousands head to Lumley and Aberdeen beaches, where police set up parking and cameras in advance. Lumley has long hosted parties and festivals, and the road from Aberdeen to Lumley, lined with restaurants and clubs, is the heart of the city’s nightlife.

traditions.title: Midnight at a service
traditions.text: Some people greet midnight and the first hours of the new year at a service in church or another place of worship.

traditions.title: Lumley and Aberdeen beaches
traditions.text: Thousands of Freetown residents spend the holidays on the ocean beaches of Lumley and Aberdeen, where bars, restaurants and clubs line the road.

traditions.title: Masquerades with a permit
traditions.text: The festive season is a time of masquerades and “mask devils”; every street outing, like any procession or carnival, is cleared with the police.

meta.title: New Year in Sierra Leone: Freetown | Time2Fest
meta.description: The first hours of 2027 in Sierra Leone pass in churches and beach bars: midnight at 00:00 UTC, crowds on Freetown’s Lumley and Aberdeen beaches, no fireworks.

TG.text:
Firecrackers crackle at midnight and the year turns over, but many Togolese have said a prayer first. About half the country is Christian, and on the night of 31 December churches are packed: vigils of worship, testimonies and prayer run from nine in the evening until one in the morning and end with a blessing and New Year wishes. Some travel to the home village to be with their elders; others spend the night in a bar or at home with family. The Guin people also keep a New Year of their own, Épé-Ékpé: every September in Glidji a sacred stone is brought out, and since 2025 these rites have been on UNESCO’s list.

Lomé greets midnight with fireworks: each year the government announces displays in the capital and in Kara. At the Colombe de la Paix roundabout the Caliente show takes over — orchestras and choirs after ten, and vuvuzelas, gongs and tam-tams until three in the morning.

traditions.title: Night of prayer
traditions.text: On 31 December churches are full from the evening: hymns, testimonies and prayers last until one in the morning, closing with a blessing and New Year wishes.

traditions.title: Fireworks and Caliente
traditions.text: Lomé and Kara meet midnight with fireworks, and at Lomé’s Colombe de la Paix roundabout orchestras, gongs and tam-tams play until 3 a.m.

traditions.title: Back to the village
traditions.text: Some families spend New Year’s night in the home village with the grandparents, others at home or in a bar, and at midnight firecrackers go off everywhere.

meta.title: New Year in Togo: Lomé | Time2Fest
meta.description: Togo meets 2027 at 00:00 UTC: church vigils until 1 a.m., fireworks over Lomé and Kara, and orchestras and tam-tams at Colombe de la Paix until 3 a.m.

IM.text:
People on the Isle of Man once called the first of January Laa Nolick beg, “Little Christmas Day”. The year began with whoever crossed the threshold first, a guest known as the qualtagh. A dark-haired man brought the most luck; he was never to arrive empty-handed, and the household set the best it had before him. That morning the floor was swept from the door towards the hearth, so as not to sweep the luck out of the house, and nothing was lent, or you would be lending all year.

On the eve, 31 December, families told fortunes: a thimble of salt was tipped onto a plate for everyone at home, and in the morning they looked to see whose little heap had fallen. On New Year’s Day young men went from house to house singing “Ollick ghennal erriu, as blein feer vie”, wishing a good year with plenty of potatoes and herring.

traditions.title: The qualtagh, first guest
traditions.text: The year’s first visitor, the qualtagh, was offered the best food in the house; a dark-haired man bearing a gift brought the most luck.

traditions.title: Salt and ash fortunes
traditions.text: On New Year’s Eve a thimble of salt was tipped onto a plate for each person at home, and in upland cottages ash was smoothed out to look for a footprint at dawn.

traditions.title: Hunt the Wren
traditions.text: On St Stephen’s Day groups singing “Hunt the Wren” carry a ribboned wren bush and dance around it; the custom was revived in the 1990s, and no bird is caught.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in the Isle of Man: Douglas | Time2Fest
meta.description: The Isle of Man greets 2027 at local midnight (00:00 UTC): the qualtagh as first guest at the door, salt-heap fortunes and an old song wishing herring.

EH.text:
“The first glass is bitter like life, the second sweet like love, the third gentle like death,” the Sahrawis say of tea. Three glasses open almost any gathering of family and friends, so New Year's Eve, too, usually passes around the teapot. Most Sahrawis are Sunni Muslims and the main feasts follow the Islamic calendar; little is known about big street celebrations on the night of 1 January. Western Sahara is a disputed territory: Morocco has de facto control of most of it, and the UN regards it as a non-self-governing territory.

Laayoune, the largest city (over 260,000 people in 2024), stands on the south bank of the dry Saguia el-Hamra riverbed. December nights here are mild — around 13 °C, never snowy. On the table: couscous, lamb or camel meat — and Spanish, a legacy of colonial times, is still heard.

traditions.title: Three glasses of tea
traditions.text: A gathering of family and friends begins with tea, drunk in three glasses, each with its own taste, from bitter to gentle. Nobody hurries over tea.

traditions.title: Couscous and mreifisa
traditions.text: The shared table holds couscous with meat and vegetables, lamb, goat or camel, and mreifisa — unleavened bread baked right in the sand.

traditions.title: A warm winter night
traditions.text: The cool Canary Current tempers the desert heat: December days reach about 24 °C and nights about 13 °C, so the year turns without snow or frost.

meta.title: New Year in Western Sahara: Laayoune | Time2Fest
meta.description: Three glasses of tea, couscous and a mild night without snow: Western Sahara meets 2027 at local midnight in Laayoune, above the Saguia el-Hamra riverbed.

AI.text:
On Anguilla the midnight fireworks go up not over a square but over the beaches. Displays light up bays all around the island, from Shoal Bay East to Meads Bay and Maundays Bay in the west, while at Sandy Ground the community puts on its own show and a beach party with music goes on until morning. Restaurants start their festive dinners early so everyone can reach the sea by midnight. Sometimes a tropical downpour gets in the way of the fireworks, but the celebration carries on.

In The Valley, the island's capital, the South Valley community sets off its own display at the primary school. And at half past ten Methodist congregations gather for the traditional Watch Night Service, saying farewell to the old year and welcoming the new one in prayer.

traditions.title: Fireworks over the beaches
traditions.text: At midnight fireworks rise over bays all around the island, from Shoal Bay East to Maundays Bay, and people greet the year right on the sand.

traditions.title: Watch Night Service
traditions.text: At 10:30 pm on 31 December Methodist congregations gather to say farewell to the old year and welcome the new one in prayer.

traditions.title: Party at Sandy Ground
traditions.text: The Sandy Ground community puts on its own fireworks, and on the beach by the beach bars people dance to music until morning.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Anguilla: The Valley | Time2Fest
meta.description: Anguilla greets 2027 at local midnight (04:00 UTC): fireworks over the beaches from Shoal Bay East to Sandy Ground and the Watch Night church service.

AW.text:
The pagara, a long ribbon of firecrackers, crackles across Aruba already in the daytime on 31 December: families and shops light it to chase away bad spirits and leave the old year behind. The better a company's year, the longer its pagara, and some burn for up to half an hour. Meanwhile dande groups go from house to house: a singer, a tambu drum, a wiri and a raspa, the chorus “ai nobe” — “new year” — and hosts drop money into the hat. People dress up even at home and follow the countdown on the radio. At midnight fireworks rise over the whole island, from Noord to San Nicolas.

Oranjestad does not rest for long: in early January, as night falls, a torch parade winds through the capital's streets and opens the carnival season.

traditions.title: A pagara against bad spirits
traditions.text: Families and companies light long ribbons of firecrackers to drive away the bad and make room for good fortune. Lightings are planned in advance so that everyone can come and watch.

traditions.title: Dande from door to door
traditions.text: Groups with a tambu, a wiri and a raspa visit relatives and friends, singing wishes of happiness and prosperity while the hosts join in the “ai nobe” chorus.

traditions.title: Ayaca on the holiday table
traditions.text: For Christmas and New Year families make ayaca: thin corn dough with stewed chicken and pork, wrapped in a banana leaf and boiled.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Aruba: Oranjestad | Time2Fest
meta.description: Aruba welcomes 2027 at local midnight (04:00 UTC): pagara firecracker ribbons against bad spirits, dande songs door to door and fireworks over the island.

PM.text:
New Year reaches Saint Pierre and Miquelon at 03:00 UTC — half an hour before neighbouring Newfoundland in Canada. The islands off its south coast belong to France, and most islanders descend from Breton, Basque and Norman fishermen, so the night is spent the French way: a festive réveillon dinner with champagne and foie gras, then «Bonne année!» and a kiss under the mistletoe at midnight. The sun sets around five, and snow at this time of year is nothing unusual.

Miquelon is the only village on its island, home to fewer than six hundred people. The archipelago's festive season starts back in November: Saint-Pierre welcomes Father Christmas in Square Joffre, and Miquelon holds a Christmas market. The holidays end at Epiphany with the galette des Rois.

traditions.title: Réveillon and mistletoe
traditions.text: On 31 December families and friends sit down to a festive dinner with champagne and foie gras, and at midnight wish each other «Bonne année!» with a kiss under the mistletoe.

traditions.title: Father Christmas and a fair
traditions.text: The festive season opens in November: in Saint-Pierre children and adults greet Father Christmas and his elves in Square Joffre, and Miquelon gathers for a Christmas market.

traditions.title: Galette des Rois
traditions.text: The holidays end at Epiphany: a galette is shared, and whoever finds the hidden bean becomes «king» or «queen» for the evening.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Saint Pierre and Miquelon | Time2Fest
meta.description: Saint Pierre and Miquelon greet 2027 at 03:00 UTC, half an hour before Newfoundland: a French réveillon with champagne, a kiss under the mistletoe, snow.

SR.text:
Owru Yari, the “old year”, is seen off in Suriname over several weeks: since 1997 the events of late December and the first days of January have been bundled into the Surifesta festival — street bars, concerts, races. The sound of the holiday is the pagara, a long red ribbon of firecrackers lit at midnight. Before that many families take a swit watra, a bath with rose and jasmine petals and a prayer, put on clean new clothes and wait for the pagara to close the year.

Paramaribo starts celebrating in daylight. On 31 December the city centre goes car-free, and from ten in the morning until six in the evening Owru Yari Fest fills Keizerstraat, Maagdenstraat and the streets around them: in 2025 the organisers expected more than 60,000 visitors and prepared over 800 metres of pagara for the relay.

traditions.title: Pagara at midnight
traditions.text: At midnight pagaras crackle all over the country — long ribbons of red firecrackers. That is how Surinamese close the old year, exchanging wishes after a prayer.

traditions.title: A swit watra flower bath
traditions.text: At the end of the year many people bathe in water with roses, jasmine and fayalobi flowers, pray for strength and prosperity, then dress in new clothes.

traditions.title: A run over the bridge
traditions.text: On the first Sunday of the new year runners take part in Bigi Broki Waka, a race across the Jules Wijdenbosch Bridge one of the Surifesta events.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Suriname: Paramaribo | Time2Fest
meta.description: Suriname welcomes 2027 at local midnight (03:00 UTC): Owru Yari with red pagara firecracker ribbons, a swit watra flower bath and a daytime fest in Paramaribo.

GF.text:
New Year's Eve in French Guiana is only the prelude to the longest carnival in the world, which begins after Epiphany and runs all the way to Ash Wednesday. The night of 31 December is above all the réveillon, when no one sleeps before midnight. Families gather around a long table of "good things from home": Creole soup, Christmas ham, game, fish and, for dessert, dizé milé — fried turnovers filled with cream. Punch and champagne go with them, and the party often lasts until morning.

Cayenne sees in the year on the Place des Palmistes: the city hosts a street ball there, local bands play until dawn, and at the stroke of midnight a twenty-minute fireworks display rises from the Jean-Martial hospital. On the night into 2026 about 16,000 people came to the square, by the organiser's count.

traditions.title: A Creole feast until morning
traditions.text: Families gather around ten in the evening: Creole soup, Christmas ham, game and fish, with dizé milé for dessert. The celebration often goes on until dawn.

traditions.title: A ball on Place des Palmistes
traditions.text: Cayenne dances at an open-air street ball, and at midnight the city's fireworks bloom over the square for twenty minutes. Firecrackers, meanwhile, were banned by the prefecture from 24 December 2024 to 9 March 2025.

traditions.title: Touloulous and galette
traditions.text: Carnival begins after Epiphany: every Saturday at the balls, touloulous covered from head to toe invite the men to dance, and each week the galette is eaten at the home of whoever found the bean.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in French Guiana: Cayenne | Time2Fest
meta.description: French Guiana welcomes 2027 at local midnight (03:00 UTC): a street ball and fireworks on Cayenne's Place des Palmistes, a Creole feast, then a long carnival.

UY.text:
White clothes, asado and twelve grapes at midnight — this is how Uruguay sees out the old year. The celebration starts at nightfall on 31 December around the family table: meat from the grill, roast suckling pig (lechón) and, for dessert, turrón and sweet pan dulce. White is worn for optimism and a clean start. At midnight everyone steps outside to set off fireworks and firecrackers. New Year falls in high summer here, so resorts such as Punta del Este fill with beach parties, music and fireworks.

Montevideo starts saying goodbye during the day. On the last working day, torn diaries and calendars fly out of office windows in the Old City — a “paper rain” — while buckets of water are poured from balconies onto passers-by. Meanwhile, by the Mercado del Puerto, a street party runs with music and a cider “battle”.

traditions.title: White clothes and grapes
traditions.text: The night is greeted in white, for optimism and a clean start, and at the stroke of midnight people eat twelve grapes.

traditions.title: Paper rain in the Old City
traditions.text: On the last working day of the year, torn calendars fly out of Montevideo’s office windows and buckets of water rain down from balconies.

traditions.title: Asado at the family table
traditions.text: On the evening of 31 December families gather: asado and lechón on the fire, turrón and pan dulce for dessert.

meta.title: New Year 2027 in Uruguay: Montevideo | Time2Fest
meta.description: Uruguay welcomes 2027 at local midnight (03:00 UTC): white clothes, asado, twelve grapes and a rain of torn calendars over the Old City of Montevideo.

AG.text:
December on Antigua once belonged to the Old Time Christmas Festival: “John Bull” masqueraders in banana leaves and animal horns roamed the streets, and carolers carried “carol trees” — poles hung with lanterns. In 1957 the festival gave way to the summer Carnival, and some of its masquerades moved to summer. The holiday table gets a glass of Ponche Kuba, a thick, sweet cream liqueur. Most islanders are Christian, and Anglicans, Moravians, Methodists and Adventists all keep the custom of a late watchnight service on 31 December, closing the year with prayer and song.

St. John’s sees the year out with a full harbour: on the last day of 2024 four cruise ships lay at its piers, and the port welcomed a record 825,000 passengers that year. On the south coast, off English Harbour, yachts set out on 31 December for the Nelson’s Pursuit Race, which re-enacts the 1805 chase of the French fleet.

traditions.title: Watchnight on 31 December
traditions.text: Anglicans, Moravians, Methodists and Adventists — the islands’ large churches — keep the late watchnight service, closing the year with prayer and hymns.

traditions.title: Nelson’s Pursuit Race
traditions.text: On 31 December yachts start off Fort Charlotte at English Harbour: slower boats go first under the French flag, and prizes are given at Nelson’s Dockyard.

traditions.title: A glass of Ponche Kuba
traditions.text: For the holidays Antiguans pour Ponche Kuba, a thick, very sweet and strong cream liqueur that is hugely popular on the festive table.

BL.text:
An island of just over ten thousand people takes in so many guests on the last night of the year that Saint Barthélemy’s hotels, villas and restaurants are full and Gustavia’s harbour gets crowded with yachts. In the evening a concert plays on the docks. As midnight strikes, fireworks light up the sky above Fort Oscar and the vessels in the harbour sound their foghorns all at once, so the new year is greeted from the shore and from the decks alike.

Gustavia, named after the Swedish King Gustav III, wraps around a horseshoe-shaped cove, and Fort Oscar stands on the hill above it, so the fireworks can be seen from the waterfronts all around. The festive season does not end on the first of January: in January the island welcomes musicians to its yearly festival.

traditions.title: Fireworks over Fort Oscar
traditions.text: The fireworks go up over Fort Oscar, a fort from the Swedish era on the hill above the harbour. People watch from the waterfront and from yacht decks.

traditions.title: Yacht horns at midnight
traditions.text: The harbour’s midnight signal is not bells but foghorns: the yachts and boats at anchor sound them all at the same moment.

traditions.title: A concert on the docks
traditions.text: New Year’s Eve in Gustavia is spent by the water: a concert plays on the docks, and the island’s restaurants and villas are fully booked.

BB.text:
“Old Year’s Night” is what Barbados calls 31 December, and people get ready well in advance. Days before, shoppers snap up shimmery dresses and suits, while barbers, hairdressers and nail technicians work through queues. South-coast restaurants take bookings for the night as early as summer. Some greet the year at a watch night service in church, others at a house lime with friends or a family dinner, and at midnight many watch fireworks over the hotels and beaches of the west coast, such as First Street in Holetown.

Bridgetown glows before the holidays: from mid-December the neo-Gothic Parliament Buildings above the Careenage are often lit in green and red. The most tireless revellers stay up for the first sunrise too: on 1 January 2023 hundreds came to a beach breakfast party at Rockfield in the north of the island.

traditions.title: Watch night in church
traditions.text: Some Barbadians spend the first minutes of the year in church, seeing the old year out with prayer and song at a watch night service.

traditions.title: Something new to wear
traditions.text: Old Year’s Night calls for new clothes: dresses and suits are bought days ahead, and barbers and hairdressers work through the queue to the last client.

traditions.title: West-coast fireworks
traditions.text: At midnight people gather by the hotels and beaches of the west coast, such as First Street in Holetown, where fireworks light up the sky.

BM.text:
Bermudians have long been nicknamed “onions”: from 1847 the islands shipped sweet Bermuda onions to the United States until exports faded out in 1946. So at midnight it is not a ball that comes down here but a papier-mâché onion wrapped in Christmas lights, in King’s Square in St George’s, the old town at the island’s east end. The Corporation of St George draws thousands there for live music from 7pm to 1am, and on the night into 2026 a show of 125 drones rose over the square after the onion for the first time. On New Year’s Day, as on Boxing Day, Gombey troupes take to the streets — dancers in masks and peacock-feather headdresses moving to drums and fife.

Hamilton, the capital above its harbour, once had an onion of its own: to welcome 2011 it was lowered over Front Street, followed by fireworks. The next year onions lit up two towns at once, Hamilton and St George’s.

traditions.title: The onion over King’s Square
traditions.text: In St George’s, a glowing papier-mâché onion is lowered over the square at midnight, a nod to islanders nicknamed “onions”.

traditions.title: Gombeys on New Year’s Day
traditions.text: Gombey troupes in masks, capes hung with mirrors and bells and peacock-feather headdresses dance through the streets to bass drum, snares and fife.

traditions.title: Cassava pie for the holidays
traditions.text: The holiday table gets cassava pie with chicken or pork, eggs and brandy, a dish dating to 1612; every family keeps its own recipe.

BQ.text:
The pagara, long ribbons of firecrackers, already roars across Bonaire, one of the three islands of the Caribbean Netherlands, in the daytime on 31 December, as shops and companies hold their own send-offs for the old year. In the evening most people gather with family and friends for festive food and music, with fireworks over the yards at midnight; some ring in the year at hotel parties. Over the December holidays ayaka, a traditional stuffed pastry, appears on menus.

On the island of Kralendijk, the first morning of the year belongs to Maskarada, one of the oldest folk customs. Groups from every village, disguised beyond recognition, come to the Lt. Governor, dance to a hand-played accordion and call out only “Bon Aña!”, receiving a bottle of rum in return. The masks come out again on the first Sunday of the year and on Three Kings.

traditions.title: Pagara in broad daylight
traditions.text: In the daytime on 31 December shops and companies light a pagara, long ribbons of firecrackers, as their own farewell to the year. The night-time fireworks belong to family yards.

traditions.title: Maskarada on 1 January
traditions.text: Masked groups, some dressed as a fish, a donkey or a bull, come to the Lt. Governor in the morning, dance to a hand-played accordion and wish a happy New Year in silence, except for a shout of “Bon Aña!”.

traditions.title: Ayaka and a family dinner
traditions.text: Most people spend New Year's Eve with family and friends, with festive food and music. During the December holidays ayaka, a traditional stuffed pastry, appears on tables and menus.
